question: Compare WHERE and HAVING in SQL, and compare inner and left joins in pandas merge.
answer: WHERE clause in SQL filters individual rows before grouping, while HAVING filters whole groups after aggregation [S1]. In SQL, the logical order of clauses is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT [S1]. WHERE clause in SQL marks NULL as a missing value [S9]. INNER JOIN in pandas merge keeps only matching keys from both tables [S8]. LEFT JOIN in pandas merge keeps every row of the left table and fills unmatched right-hand columns with NaN [S8].

citations.title: Data Wrangling Handbook
citations.text:
3. Combining Tables
pd.merge joins two DataFrames on key columns. The default is an inner join, which keeps only
keys present in both tables. A left join keeps every row of the left table and fills unmatched
right-hand columns with NaN.
If a key is duplicated in both tables the result contains every pairing of the matching rows, so the
row count can grow (a many-to-many join). pd.concat stacks tables; by default it stacks vertically
(axis=0).

S2.title: Data Wrangling Handbook
S2.text:
1. Selecting Rows and Columns
In pandas, df.loc selects by label and df.iloc selects by integer position. A label slice such as
df.loc['a':'c'] includes the end label 'c', whereas a position slice such as df.iloc[0:3] excludes position
3.
Boolean masks such as df[df['amount'] > 100] keep the rows where the condition is true.
df.query('amount > 100') expresses the same filter as a string.

S5.title: Data Wrangling Handbook
S5.text:
2. Missing Values
pandas represents missing numbers as NaN. isna() flags them, dropna() removes rows with any
missing value by default, and fillna(value) replaces them. NaN is not equal to itself, so a
comparison such as x == np.nan is never true; use isna() instead.
In SQL the missing marker is NULL, and a comparison with NULL is unknown, so use IS NULL
rather than = NULL. Aggregations such as AVG ignore NULL values; the pandas mean() skips
NaN by default (skipna=True).
